title: BEFORE YOU JUDGE THE COLOR OF THEIR SKIN, REMEMBER WHO PUT HIS IMAGE BENEATH IT
paragraphs: BEFORE YOU JUDGE THE COLOR OF THEIR SKIN, REMEMBER WHO PUT HIS IMAGE BENEATH IT
You can know Bible verses, sing worship songs, defend Christian doctrine—and still need Jesus to confront the way you see another human being.
There is a terrifying possibility that nobody likes talking about.
You can hold a Bible in your hand...
and prejudice in your heart.
You can sing about the blood of Jesus on Sunday and look down on somebody because of the color of their skin on Monday.
You can say, “God loves everyone,” and still feel uncomfortable when your child befriends someone from another ethnicity.
You can post Scripture.
You can wear a cross.
You can know Christian language.
You can even tell people how long you have been saved.

And still, somewhere beneath the religious vocabulary, there can be a corner of the heart where another person has been reduced to a color, an accent, a nationality, a tribe, a surname, or a stereotype.
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve the language coming out of our mouths.
He came to transform the heart producing it.
And before this article is finished, perhaps the question will no longer be, “Are other people racist?”
Perhaps the question will become much closer.
“Lord... is there something in me You still need to crucify?”
Go all the way back to the beginning.
Before nations.
Before borders.
Before flags.
Before the labels humanity would eventually use to divide itself.
Genesis says:
“וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ”
Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam betsalmo...
“And God created humankind in His image...”
Genesis 1:27.
The Hebrew expression בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — betselem Elohim means “in the image of God.”
Stop there.
Before Scripture tells you a person’s nationality, social status, accomplishments, education, wealth, or appearance, Scripture gives humanity an astonishing dignity:
Image-bearer.
The person you were taught to distrust bears the image of God.
The person whose skin is darker than yours bears the image of God.
The person whose skin is lighter than yours bears the image of God.
The person whose accent sounds strange to you bears the image of God.
The immigrant.
The foreigner.
The neighbor.
The stranger.
The person from the ethnic group your family mocked when you were growing up.
The person whose people have historically hurt your people.
None of this means every culture, belief, action, ideology, or behavior is morally equivalent. Scripture never teaches that.
It means something deeper.
Human worth is not distributed according to pigmentation.
God never gave us permission to measure human dignity with a color chart.

And racism becomes especially grotesque when it enters the heart of someone claiming allegiance to Jesus, because the Christian is supposed to look at another human being through the revelation of God—not through inherited contempt.
Sometimes prejudice arrives loudly.
Sometimes it wears a hood.
Sometimes it screams slurs.
Sometimes it commits violence.
But sometimes it is much quieter.
Sometimes it sounds like a joke everyone in the family laughs at.
Sometimes it is the hesitation before sitting beside someone.
Sometimes it is the assumption that “those people” are all the same.
Sometimes it is the person you would happily evangelize but would never want your daughter to marry simply because of ethnicity.
Sometimes it is treating one group’s failures as individual failures while treating another group’s failures as proof of what “they” are all like.
Sometimes nobody else can see it.
But God can.
That is what makes Scripture dangerous to our pride.
The Bible does not merely give us ammunition for confronting everybody else.
It turns the blade toward us.
James wrote:
“Ἀδελφοί μου, μὴ ἐν προσωπολημψίαις ἔχετε τὴν πίστιν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ...”
“My brothers, do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ... with partiality.”
James 2:1.
The Greek word is striking: προσωπολημψίαις — prosōpolēmpsiais.
It speaks of partiality—showing favoritism based on outward status or appearance.
James was addressing favoritism toward rich and poor, not writing a modern essay about race. We should respect that context.
But then James drives the principle deeper.
“If you show partiality, you commit sin.”
James 2:9.
Not merely bad manners.
Not merely cultural insensitivity.
Sin.
That should disturb us.
Because Christianity gives us no safe category where contempt for another image-bearer becomes acceptable simply because everybody around us learned the same contempt.
Maybe your grandfather said it.
Maybe your parents believed it.
Maybe your neighborhood normalized it.
Maybe your friends laughed about it.
Maybe your culture handed it to you before you were old enough to examine it.
But inherited sin does not become holiness simply because it has been in the family for generations.
At some point Jesus stands in front of every inherited darkness and says:
Follow Me.
Not your prejudice.
Not your tribe.
Not your pride.
Me.
Paul stood in Athens among people separated by geography, history, religion, and culture and declared something extraordinary about humanity:
“ἐποίησέν τε ἐξ ἑνὸς πᾶν ἔθνος ἀνθρώπων...”
Acts 17:26.
Literally, the crucial phrase ἐξ ἑνὸς — ex henos means “from one.”
From one, God made every nation of humanity.

There is an important manuscript detail worth knowing rather than hiding: some later Greek manuscripts add αἵματος — haimatos, “blood,” which is why older English translations such as the KJV famously say God “hath made of one blood all nations of men.” The critical Greek text simply has “from one.”
Either way, Paul’s argument destroys racial boasting.
Humanity does not consist of separate classes of human worth.
We share a common human origin under one Creator.
Different nations?
Yes.
Different peoples?
Yes.
Different languages?
Absolutely.
Different histories, traditions, foods, music, clothing, experiences, and cultures?
Of course.
Scripture does not erase human diversity.
It refuses to turn diversity into a hierarchy of human value.
And then something even greater happens at the cross.
Jesus does not merely tell hostile human beings to tolerate one another.
He creates a redeemed people.
Paul writes:
“There is neither Jew nor Greek... for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”
Galatians 3:28.
Read that carefully.
Paul is not claiming Jewish people stopped being Jewish or Greeks stopped being Greek.
The New Testament continues recognizing ethnic and cultural identities.
He is declaring that those distinctions cannot determine someone’s standing before God or superiority within Christ.
εἷς ἐστε — heis este.
“You are one.”
Not identical.
One.
The Gospel does not produce a colorless humanity.
It produces a reconciled humanity whose deepest identity is found in Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes people try to defeat racism by pretending differences do not exist.
Scripture gives us something more beautiful.
God sees nations.
God sees peoples.
God sees languages.
God sees tribes.
And He redeems people from among them.
John was permitted to see where history is going.
He looked toward the throne and saw:
“ἐκ παντὸς ἔθνους καὶ φυλῶν καὶ λαῶν καὶ γλωσσῶν...”
“from every nation and tribes and peoples and languages...”
Revelation 7:9.
Do you see it?
Heaven is not embarrassed by human diversity.
The redeemed multitude does not appear as one earthly ethnicity that defeated all the others.
Every nation.
Every tribe.
Every people.
Every language.
Standing before one throne.
Worshiping one Lamb.
Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing there someday.
Imagine seeing faces from peoples you never encountered on earth.
Languages you never understood.
Cultures you never experienced.
People your ancestors may once have called enemies.
People history separated.
People politics divided.
People wars taught to hate each other.
And there they are.
Redeemed.
White robes.
One Savior.
One song.
One Lamb.
Then imagine having to remember that while you were on earth, you once believed your skin somehow made you better than theirs.
How small our prejudice will look before the throne of God.
How embarrassing our superiority will become beneath the glory of the Lamb.
And here is where the Gospel refuses to leave us merely ashamed.
Because Christianity is not simply the announcement that racism is wrong.
If that were the whole message, we would leave convicted but unchanged.
The Gospel goes further.
It says the racist can repent.
The hateful can be forgiven.
The wounded can begin healing.
The proud can be humbled.
The bitter can surrender their bitterness.
The person who spent decades despising another group can receive a new heart.
Because Jesus Christ did not die only for respectable sins.
He died for sinners.
There may be someone reading this who has carried racial hatred for years.
Maybe you know exactly where it began.
Somebody hurt you.
Somebody humiliated you.
Someone from another ethnicity betrayed your family.
Perhaps history itself wounded your people.
And slowly pain became generalization.
Generalization became suspicion.
Suspicion became resentment.
Resentment became hatred.
Eventually you stopped seeing individuals.
You saw categories.
But listen carefully.
What happened to you may have been evil.
The Gospel never requires us to pretend injustice did not happen.
Forgiveness does not rename evil as good.
But another person's sin does not give us permission to surrender our heart to hatred.
Jesus can heal what hatred has occupied.
Maybe your story is different.
Nobody traumatized you.
You simply inherited prejudice.
You heard the jokes at the dinner table.
You heard the comments in the car.
You watched adults recoil from certain people.
Nobody sat you down and taught you a doctrine of racial superiority.
They didn't have to.
Children learn what adults repeatedly communicate.
And years later you became an adult carrying assumptions you never consciously chose.
Now Christ is exposing them.
Do not run from that moment.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction can be mercy knocking on a locked room.
Open it.
Let Jesus inside.
Say it plainly.
“Lord Jesus, I have judged people You created.”
“I have carried contempt.”
“I have laughed when I should have spoken.”
“I have stereotyped people I never even knew.”
“I have allowed bitterness to become prejudice.”
“Forgive me.”
That prayer is not weakness.
That is where freedom begins.
The Hebrew Scriptures gave Israel this command:
“וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ”
Ve’ahavta lere’akha kamokha.
“You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Leviticus 19:18.
Jesus later identified love for neighbor as one of the great commandments.
Not tolerate your neighbor.
Not merely avoid attacking your neighbor.
Love.
And Christian love is not sentimental blindness.
It seeks another person's good because that person matters before God.
So perhaps the next step after reading this is not posting an angry argument.
Perhaps it is repentance.
Perhaps it is calling somebody.
Perhaps it is listening.
Perhaps it is apologizing for the joke you thought was harmless.
Perhaps it is teaching your children something healthier than what you inherited.
Perhaps it is refusing to forward the degrading meme.
Perhaps it is defending someone when everybody else expects you to laugh.
Perhaps it is looking into the face of someone you were conditioned to distrust and remembering:
Image-bearer.
And perhaps the hardest person to confront today is not “the racist people out there.”
Perhaps it is the person in the mirror.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't perform for anybody.
Be honest before Christ.
Someone who thinks people never change may need to see evidence of grace.
There should be no shame in admitting that healing is still happening.
Grace works in real people with real scars.
Not because sharing a Facebook article makes somebody righteous.
It doesn't.
Someone may have been wounded by racism and quietly wondering whether Christianity has anything better to offer.
Someone may need to discover that Jesus does not belong to one race.
Not merely because you agree with it today, but because prejudice has a way of hiding behind new language. Return to the Scriptures. Test your heart again.
But I also want to ask something deeper of those who believe this work should continue.
Gospel ministry requires people willing to carry it.
Some preach.
Some write.
Some pray.
Some share.
Some give.
Some quietly help make it possible for the message to reach the next person.
But please understand this biblically.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Christian generosity is supposed to come from a willing heart. Paul wrote:
“μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης”
mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs
“not reluctantly or under compulsion.”
2 Corinthians 9:7.
So if you support Gospel Warrior, do it freely.
Do it prayerfully.
Do it because you believe spreading Scripture, Gospel-centered discipleship, Christian resources, and the message of Jesus is worth supporting.

Financially supporting faithful Gospel work can be one way we use what God has entrusted to us for His glory—but giving must never become a transaction in which we imagine we are purchasing God's favor.
Pray.
Send it privately to someone who needs it.
Let truth travel farther than hatred.
Let Scripture speak louder than stereotypes.
Let the Gospel go where prejudice has lived for generations.
Because racism will never finally be defeated merely by teaching people which words they are forbidden to say.
The heart itself must change.
And only Jesus Christ can take a heart filled with pride, hatred, bitterness, fear, tribal superiority, and inherited darkness...
and make it new.
At the foot of the cross, nobody gets to boast about the color of the skin covering their body.
We boast in Christ.
At the throne, redeemed humanity will not be celebrating which race conquered the others.
Every nation, tribe, people, and language will be looking toward the same Lamb.
So the next time you are tempted to judge someone because their skin does not look like yours, remember something eternity will make impossible to forget:
The skin you almost used as a reason to despise them is wrapped around a human being God commanded you to love—and a soul for whom Christ is mighty to save.
